newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O. LICHT - Daily coffee report.
newsitem.headline: F.O. LICHT - Daily coffee report.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London finished broadly lower pounded by persistent origin selling but spot November bucked the trend and ended firmer on short-covering. Benchmark January rose to a high of $1,445 a tonne before settling $19 down at $1,430 but November firmed $21 at $1,565. The November/January spread, a barometer of nearby supply availability, widened again to $135 at the close, up from $100 on Wednesday. The slide in London accelerated in early afternoon after New York losses on commission house selling. Arabica futures in New York fell to its lowest level in more than two weeks, as views a recent supply crunch appeared to be coming to an end touched off successive waves of speculative and producer selling, industry sources said. The benchmark March contract fell to a low of 108.85 cents/lb but traders said it could regain support at 110 cents. Upside resistance is seen at 115 cents.

COSTA RICA - Costa Rica recently revised its 1996/97 coffee crop down to 2.28 million 60-kg bags due to damage from hurricane Caesar, which swept across Central America in late July. Previously the country expected to produce 2.38 million 60-kg bags.

IVORY COAST - Ivorian Prime Minister Daniel Kablan Duncan recently said that he expected the country's coffee crop to total at least 200,000 tonnes in 1996/96, up from around 170,000 tonnes last season. The expected improvement in Ivorian coffee output follows a 32 billion CFA revival plan, favourable crop weather and better maintenance of coffee plantations.

BRAZIL - Brazil's 1997/98 coffee crop could see a fall of 20 per cent on the 1996/97 harvest, according to preliminary estimates by an agronomist at the Sao Paulo Institute of Agricultural Economics. According to Luiz Moricochi, the crop could reach no more than 19.2 million bags, against 24 million bags in 1996/97. Moricochi based his forecast on interviews with agronomists and growers throughout the key coffee growing regions in Brazil. However, he cautioned that it is only preliminary data and that a clearer picture will emerge in January and February. Moricochi is responsible for coordinating forecasts for the state of Sao Paulo, with the institute currently conducting surveys for the 1997/98 harvest in the state which should be ready in December.

CANADA - Coffee imports in July 1996 amounted to 209,443 bags, up from last year's 185,686 bags. This brought cumulative imports in the first seven months of 1996 (January/July) up to 1.58 million bags, almost 13 per cent up on the tonnage imported in the corresponding period the previous year. Total imports in 1995 reached 2.51 million tonnes against 2.83 million tonnes in 1994. Major suppliers of green coffee in January/July 1996 were Colombia (271,900 vs 199,400 bags), Mexico (203,700 vs 100,000 bags) and Guatemala (154,000 vs 122,600 bags). The United States continued to be the largest supplier of roast and ground coffee, delivering 232,200 vs 225,500 bags. Coffee exports in July 1996 reached 18,032 bags, which brought cumulative exports in January/July 1996 up to 179,396 bags, 5.5 per cent up on last year's 169,976 bags. Total exports in 1995 reached 303,845 bags compared to 334,419 bags exported in 1994. Canada exports most of its coffee in the form of solubles with the USA (130,200 vs 131,900 bags) being the main market.
